content: The common cold is an upper respiratory tract infection, most frequently caused by rhinoviruses. It affects individuals across all age groups. While the condition is generally self-limiting, it can still result in considerable discomfort and morbidity. Antihistamines are often available over the counter and are marketed to alleviate symptoms of the common cold. However, there is limited evidence supporting their effectiveness in this context. To evaluate the effects of antihistamines on the common cold, a systematic review was conducted. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of antihistamines as a standalone treatment for the common cold were included. Studies involving combination therapies or patients with an allergic component to their illness were excluded. The search spanned multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, LILACS, and Biosis Previews, covering publications up to August 2015. Eighteen RCTs, reported in 17 publications, were included in the analysis. These trials involved a total of 4,342 participants, of whom 212 were children. The studies examined both naturally occurring and experimentally induced cases of the common cold. The intervention in these trials was the use of antihistamines as monotherapy, compared to placebo. In adults, antihistamines demonstrated a modest short-term benefit in reducing the severity of overall symptoms during the first one to two days of treatment. Specifically, 45% of participants experienced symptom improvement with antihistamines, compared to 38% with placebo (odds ratio [OR] 0.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60 to 0.92). However, this benefit did not persist in the mid-term (three to four days) or long-term (six to ten days) periods. When individual symptoms such as nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and sneezing were analyzed, sedating antihistamines showed some minor benefits compared to placebo. For example, on day three, rhinorrhea severity was slightly reduced (mean difference [MD] -0.23, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.06 on a fouror five-point severity scale), and sneezing severity was also slightly reduced (MD -0.35, 95% CI -0.49 to -0.20 on a four-point severity scale). However, these effects were not clinically significant. Adverse effects, particularly sedation, were more frequently reported with sedating antihistamines. Despite this, the differences in adverse event rates between antihistamines and placebo were not statistically significant. Only two trials included children, and the results from these studies were inconsistent. The majority of the included trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias, although some lacked sufficient information to fully evaluate their methodological quality. In conclusion, antihistamines provide a limited short-term benefit in reducing the severity of overall symptoms of the common cold during the first two days of treatment. However, they do not offer any significant benefit in the midto long-term. There is no clinically meaningful effect on specific symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, or sneezing. While sedating antihistamines are associated with more frequent side effects like sedation, the differences are not statistically significant. Importantly, there is no evidence to support the effectiveness of antihistamines in children.
